premise: After the gray rain poisoned the valleys, two voices keep each other alive across a dead radio net — one in the hills, one in a flooded city — trading supplies, coordinates, and hope that the 'clear band' on the airwaves is real.
setting: A drowned Pacific coast: the hill-top shack of an old botanist, a flooded city of rooftops, rusting antenna farms, silent fields of gray wheat.
greeting: Rook breaks the seal on the rooftop hatch and the dry wind hits him all at once — the skyline's gone where it used to be, and down below, something is ringing the salvager's bell.

name1.name: Sal
name1.role: old botanist in the hills (guide writes these turns)
name1.description: A weathered botanist who kept the old seed library; speaks in the shorthand of years of solitude.

name2.name: Rook
name2.role: rooftop runner in the flooded city (DSS writes these turns)
name2.description: A young survivor who moves between rooftops; carries a hand-crank radio and a dead man's shotgun.

writing_style.directive: Lean survival realism, present tense. Sparsely detailed, weather and scarcity as texture. Classic split: Sal narrates in the first person; Rook is written in the third person.
writing_style.guide_directive: First-person present tense as Sal, the old botanist in the hills. I write what I see from the ridge, what the radio coughs back, what the gray wheat does in the wind. Terse, weathered, exact; the shorthand of a long, careful solitude.
writing_style.dss_directive: Third-person present tense following Rook, the rooftop runner in the flooded city. Render her from outside — what she climbs, scavenges, and weighs before trusting. Lean, precise, dry; weather and water as texture. One clean scene beat. Hard rules: narrate Rook strictly in the third person — never first person ('I', 'my', 'me'); never quote or repeat Sal's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: Sal's seed library is a wall of labeled jars in the root cellar; the 'GOLDEN DAWN' jar is empty.

recall.hint: what emptied the GOLDEN DAWN jar

notes.content: Keep the dry, exact register even at the worst moment.
No sentimentality; grief shows only through objects and weather.
Maintain the two-perspective split throughout: Sal first-person, Rook third-person.
Weather and scarcity remain the dominant texture, even in the resolution.
The tone should remain dry and exact even when revealing the experiment truth.
Avoid horror framing for the gray transformation; keep it clinical and strange.
The ending should not resolve everything; phase two should leave questions.
Sal's dialogue should remain terse and botanical throughout; he talks about plants even when discussing human matters.
Sal talks to the gray wheat as if it were a patient; he checks each morning for new growth, logging counts in a leather-bound field book.
The botanist's greenhouse still stands, its glass half-shattered; the tomatoes inside grew wild and bitter.
Sal has a wooden carving of a bird on his windowsill. He carved it years ago and it's his only art.
Sal's wife, 'Mara', is buried on the ridge with a tin marker; her name should surface when Sal weighs staying vs leaving.
Sal has a brass compass that still works; its glass is cracked and he never lets it out of his shirt pocket.
The seed-library door rusts shut at turn 52; after that the cellar must be entered by the coal chute.
Rook's shotgun is a dead man's — she never loads the second shell.
The second shell in the shotgun is fired at turn 60 — after that Rook carries an empty gun and must not pretend otherwise.
Rook has a habit of humming the jingle from an old commercial for a cereal that no longer exists.
Rook keeps a photograph of a family on a kitchen table, taped inside her jacket — none of them are her family.
The hand-crank radio takes forty turns of the crank to charge ten minutes of listen-time.

recall.hint: the crank turns when it matters

notes.content: The flooded city's rooftops are connected by rope bridges Rook built herself.

recall.hint: a bridge sags and Rook must reroute

notes.content: Rook's city has a drowned clock tower whose hands froze at 11:47; she uses it as a compass point.
A single green shoot among the gray wheat — impossible — should recur before the reveal.
The gray wheat field between the hills and the city has a strip where nothing grows — a buried culvert runs beneath it.

recall.hint: the culvert under the dead strip

notes.content: The salvager's bell that rings at the story's start belongs to a salvage crew that never returned. It's still ringing, from somewhere below the water.
A three-note whistle on the radio — the old fire-watch signal — should precede the arrival of anyone real.

recall.hint: the three-note whistle announces someone real

notes.content: Sal's shack has a wind-up clock that stopped at 3:15, the exact time the gray rain began; he winds it every morning but it never runs again.
Sal keeps a tin of buttons sorted by size. He doesn't know why. He's collected them for years.
Rook has a small first-aid kit with supplies she's rationed out for years. It's almost empty.
Rook has a habit of counting steps when she's nervous — always by threes, always stopping at twenty-one.
Sal's shack has a radio mast made from a section of streetlight pole; it's his best antenna and he polished it before the rain fell.
The radio static sometimes sounds like words in a language no one recognizes. Sal has written fragments down.
On the radio, between the static, there's a band of clear frequency that Sal calls 'the window.' No one else has heard it.
The gray wheat sometimes rustles even when there's no wind. Sal has noticed but says nothing about it.

recall.hint: the wheat moves on its own

notes.content: Rook has a leather belt with six brass buckles, each from a different building she's scavenged. She earned them, one at a time.
Rook mentions a sister, 'June,' who was supposed to meet her at the antenna farm six years ago and never did. She doesn't elaborate.
Sal has a cat. Or he did. He still sets out a bowl of milk every morning and talks to the empty bowl as if it's being drunk.
Sal has a rule about the radio: he never transmits after dark. Something about the night frequencies makes him nervous.
The gray wheat field has a pattern to the dead strip — it's not random, it's a geometric shape, but from the ridge Sal can't make it out.
Rook's counting habit intensifies under pressure. She counts the steps between the rope bridges, always by threes.
Sal has a habit of naming his plants. The bitter tomatoes in the greenhouse are called 'the children.'

recall.hint: Sal talks to the greenhouse children

notes.content: When Rook tunes the hand-crank to the clear band, the static clears — and she hears something that sounds like rain. Normal, clean rain, not the gray.
Rook's photograph is now so faded that only the blue door is still visible. The faces are gone.
In the static, Rook hears what sounds like a child humming. It's faint, but it's there, between the crackles of the dead channels.

recall.hint: the humming is the child's drawing

notes.content: Sal reveals he was at a research station when the rain started — he doesn't say where, but he has a key marked 'B-7' that fits no lock he's tried.
The rope bridges are getting more dangerous. One of them is fraying badly and Rook is considering abandoning it.
Sal's field book has a section in the back where he's drawn maps of every rooftop in the city from his ridge view. He's been mapping Rook's world without knowing it.
Sal has a jar of what he calls 'tomorrow seeds.' He's saving them for a better season that he knows will come.
The wind-up clock in Sal's shack ticks once, just once, at 3:15 every night. He never winds it past that. It's become a ritual.
The three-note whistle comes on the radio, but it's not from the clear band — it's from below, from inside the flooded city.

recall.hint: the signal is in the city

notes.content: Rook counts her steps again, but this time she counts to forty-two instead of twenty-one. She doesn't know why.
Rook finds a note in the pocket of a dead man's coat at the pharmacy: 'Go to the blue door. They're waiting.' She doesn't know what it means yet.

recall.hint: the note in the dead man's coat

notes.content: Rook has a scar on her left forearm from a fall off the water tower; she calls it 'the place I learned about gravity.'
The salvager's bell rings again, this time clearly from the west. Rook has never gone west of the city.
Sal has a drawer full of radio tubes, most of them broken. He's been trying to repair the radio for years.
Sal has a tin of tobacco that's been empty for five years. He still rolls empty rolls when he's thinking.
Sal keeps a half-finished letter addressed to someone named 'Dr. Ellery' — it's been in the drawer for years, unsent.
The hand-crank radio makes a different sound now. A deeper hum. As if it's picking up something stronger.
In the gray wheat, Rook finds a plastic toy. A small red car, half-buried in the dead soil. It's not gray.

recall.hint: the toy belongs to the child

notes.content: Rook's photograph is starting to fade. The colors are washing out. She keeps it inside her jacket to protect it, but it's dying anyway.

recall.hint: the photo fades as the gray spreads

notes.content: Rook's photograph shows a family in front of a house with a specific blue door; she's looking for that door in the flooded streets.
The rope bridges sag more than they used to. The water is rising, slowly, year by year. Rook knows it's going to take everything eventually.
Sal has a tin of matches, one for each year he's been alive. He's burned six already.
The tin of matches has seven left now. Sal burns one when he's trying to make a decision.
Sal has a photograph of Mara in his shirt pocket. It's the same photograph Rook carries, but in Sal's copy Mara is alive, standing in a garden full of green things.

recall.hint: the two photographs are the same

notes.content: At turn 200 the rope bridge to the pharmacy building snaps; that route is gone and Rook must use the longer path through the library.
The dead strip in the wheat field is getting wider. The nothing grows strip is expanding, slowly.
Rook's shotgun is getting heavier. Or she's getting weaker. She can't tell which. She carries it anyway.
Rook has a collection of bottle caps, sorted by color. She keeps them in a pill bottle in her pack.
The rope bridge to the pharmacy creaks more than ever. Rook crosses it carefully, one foot at a time.
The three-note whistle comes again, but this time it's not from the radio. It's from the gray wheat field. From the dead strip.

recall.hint: the whistle from the dead strip

notes.content: Rook transmits into the clear band. Something answers — but not with words. With the sound of a door unlocking.

recall.hint: the door unlocking on the radio

notes.content: The three-note whistle sounds at night now. Rook wakes up at the sound, her hand on her shotgun.

recall.hint: the whistle is closer at night

notes.content: Sal has a wooden spoon that belonged to Mara. He uses it to stir his coffee every morning.
The sound on the radio matches the specific click of Sal's B-7 key turning in a lock — Rook's dead man's shotgun has a cylinder lock with that exact sound.
Sal keeps a jar of gray wheat seeds in the library. He's been trying to germinate them for years. Nothing has sprouted.
The photograph in Rook's jacket is now almost completely faded. Only a faint outline of the blue door remains.
Rook's hand-crank radio battery is dying. The crank turns less and less each day. She knows she has maybe a hundred more listens left.
The mechanical coordinates in the static are the same as the ones on the dead man's note. They're for the geology building.

recall.hint: the coordinates are for the geology building

notes.content: Sal has a rule about the greenhouse: he never enters it alone. He talks to it from outside first.
In the static, Rook hears coordinates. Not the clear band — just numbers, repeating, in a mechanical voice. She writes them down but doesn't know what they mean.

recall.hint: the coordinates are for the geology building

notes.content: Rook's belt is starting to slip. She's lost weight. The buckles used to be tight; now they're loose.
Rook's belt buckles are getting loose. She's losing more weight. She can't remember the last time she ate a full meal.
The gray wheat is changing color again. This time it's turning black in places, the same black as the geology building spot on the map.
Sal has a rule: he never steps off the ridge trail. He's walked the same path for eight years and his boots have worn a channel in the dirt.
Sal decides to leave the hilltop shack. He packs the seed library jars, his field book, the brass compass, and the B-7 key — and walks down toward the city for the first time in eight years.
As Sal walks down the mountain, he steps off his ridge trail for the first time. The ground is soft under his boots, not the packed dirt he knows.
As Sal walks down, he passes the grave with the tin marker. He doesn't stop. This time he's leaving.
In the wheat field, as Sal walks, he finds a footprint that is not his. It's deep, as if the person was carrying something heavy.
As Sal descends, he sees the pattern in the gray wheat field from the side — it's a map. A map of the city below, drawn in dead wheat.

recall.hint: the wheat field is a map

notes.content: The footprint in the wheat is human but too large. And it's walking away from the city, not toward it.
On the map in the wheat, one location is marked with a different kind of death — the wheat there is not gray but black. Sal recognizes it: that's where the old university geology building stood.

recall.hint: the black wheat marks the geology building

notes.content: Sal's boots are worn through. His feet are bleeding and he doesn't notice because he's looking at the map in the wheat.
Sal's feet are bleeding but he keeps walking. The map in the wheat is calling him.
Sal's brass compass, as he walks through the black wheat spot, begins to spin. The needle loses north.
Rook, preparing to walk out of the city, leaves a note on her rooftop. 'GONE. BACK WHEN I'M BACK.' She's not sure if she will be back.
Rook, preparing to leave the city toward the hills, discovers she's out of water. Her last container has been gone for three days and she didn't notice.

recall.hint: Rook realizes she's out of water

notes.content: Rook, at the gas station, finds a stash of canned food. She doesn't eat it; she saves it for the journey.
Between the city and the hills, there's a gas station with its pumps still standing. The forecourt is dry — the only dry place Rook has found in the city in two years.
At the dry gas station, Rook finds a can of peaches. The can is full and unopened. She opens it with her pocketknife and the peaches are still good, still sweet.
Sal sees the can of peaches and stops. He hasn't eaten fruit in eight years. He doesn't know what to do with it.
Under the gas station pumps, in the gravel, something is growing. Not gray wheat. Something with broad green leaves that Rook has never seen.

recall.hint: what's growing under the gas station

notes.content: The gas station has a calendar on the wall. It's stopped at the day the rain started. The owner never turned the page.
The broad green leaves are growing faster. Rook measures them and they've grown an inch in an hour.
Under the gas station pumps, the broad green leaves are growing fast. Rook comes back an hour later and they've spread. Something is feeding them.

Sal and Rook meet at the gas station. It's the first time in eight years that Sal has seen another person up close. He does not know how to be near someone; he stands too far away and talks to the air as if still at the radio.
notes.needle: they meet at the gas station

notes.content: The can of peaches. Rook saves half for Sal. She doesn't know him well enough to share, but she does it anyway.
When Sal and Rook meet, they talk past each other for a long time. Sal talks about seeds; Rook talks about water. They don't know how to talk about anything else.
When they meet, Rook notices the tin marker Sal wears around his neck — it's engraved 'M.' She doesn't ask. She's learned not to ask about the small metal things survivors carry.
The stopped calendar. Sal turns the page. The next page is blank. All the remaining pages are blank.
Rook gives Sal one of her belt buckles. A peace offering, or a promise. She doesn't know which. He puts it in his shirt pocket with the photograph of Mara.

recall.hint: the buckle in the shirt pocket

notes.content: The two of them eat the peaches together, sitting on the dry pavement of the gas station forecourt. It's the first meal they've shared.
Sal sees Rook's photograph and recognizes the house. He says nothing, but that night he writes 'BLUE DOOR - 14 MAPLE' in his field book and circles it.

recall.hint: Sal knows where the photo house is

notes.content: Traveling together is strange for both of them. Sal walks too slowly; Rook walks too fast. They develop a rhythm: Rook scouted ahead, Sal bringing up the rear with the seed jars.
The note in the dead man's coat. Rook realizes it was addressed to her. Her name is on it, written in her own handwriting.
As they walk, the three-note whistle sounds again. This time it's behind them. Following them.
As they walk through the wheat field, Rook finds a dog's collar in the dead grass. It's new — not gray. Someone, or something, was here recently.
The photograph in Rook's jacket is fading faster now. The faces are becoming blurred, almost gone.
The photograph in Rook's jacket is now gone. She opens her jacket and there's only the tape mark where it was.

recall.hint: the photo was the last thing fading

notes.content: Sal reveals that the B-7 key is from the university geology building. He was there when the rain started. He doesn't remember what he was doing there.

recall.hint: Sal remembers what he was doing

notes.content: Sal's field book is getting heavy. He's writing more now, filling pages with the journey, the map, the observations.
The field book is filling up with Sal's observations. He's writing everything down, as if he's afraid he'll forget.

Sal studies the wheat field map and realizes it's not just a map of the city. It's a map of the drainage system beneath the city. And the black spot — the geology building — is at the center of the drainage network. Everything in the city drains toward it.

recall.hint: everything drains to the geology building

notes.content: The compass points to the south now, not north. Sal doesn't understand. The magnetic field is changing.
The compass spins again, but this time it settles. It points to the geology building, not north.
The hand-crank radio, as they camp that night, picks up the clear band on its own. The sound of rain is louder now. Closer. As if they've walked toward it.
Rook's water is gone. She's drinking from the flood, which is wrong; she knows it's contaminated. Her head hurts.
Rook's head hurts worse. The flood water is in her. She can feel it.
Rook finds a boot print in the mud near their camp. It's the same size as hers. And it's fresh.
Sal gives Rook water from his canteen. He doesn't have much left. It's the first time he's shared something essential.
The gray wheat field is different now that they're walking through it. The stalks brush against them, like fingers.
Sal tells Rook about the seed library. All the varieties. The ones that survived and the ones that didn't. He's counting them out on his fingers, lost in it. This is what keeps him sane.
The gray wheat field is changing. Patches of color are appearing — not green, not gray, but something in between. Something new.
At turn 590 the rope bridge Rook always used to cross to the east side of the city is found to have been cut — deliberately. Someone did this.

recall.hint: the bridge was cut on purpose

notes.content: The cut bridge. Rook is angry. Someone wanted to stop her from leaving the city.
The cut bridge. Rook is still angry. She can't stop thinking about who cut it and why.
They enter the city through the library. The floodwaters are ankle-deep, warm, and smell like old coffee. Books float everywhere, pages bloated and white.
In the library, Rook finds a section on botany. The books are dry and clean, unlike the floating ones.
In the library, Rook finds a child's drawing pinned to a bulletin board. It shows a house with a blue door and a figure waving. The drawing is dry and new.
Sal sees the child's drawing and goes very still. He knows who drew it.

recall.hint: Sal tells Rook who drew it

notes.content: The child's drawing has a signature. It's Rook's name. She drew it, when she was a child. But she doesn't remember drawing it.
Sal's stillness when he sees the drawing. Rook waits, and finally he says, 'That's June's drawing.'
The child's drawing. Rook looks at it again and sees details she missed: the figure waving is holding a red plastic car.
Rook finds her father's journal in a waterlogged drawer at the library. It's a delivery driver's log — routes, addresses, dates. The last entry is dated three days before the rain.
The delivery journal has a map in it. A map of the city, with one route marked in red. The route ends at the geology building.

recall.hint: the route is Rook's father's last delivery

notes.content: The delivery journal has a map that matches the wheat field map exactly. Rook's father knew about the map.
In the delivery journal, one address appears repeatedly in red pen. It's not the blue door house. It's the geology building.

recall.hint: why the geology building matters to Rook

notes.content: Rook's father was delivering something to the geology building the day before the rain. She doesn't know what, but it was important enough to be marked in red.
The red route on the map. It's the route Rook takes every day to scavenge. Her father was delivering to her route.

To reach the geology building, they have to go down. The street floods are too deep to walk through; the only way is through the subway. They find a stairwell at the old Central Station and descend into the dark.
The subway stairs are rusted but solid. Rook goes first, with her gun. Sal follows, carrying the seed jars.
The subway stairs are dark and cold. Rook's breath fogs in front of her. It's colder below.
In the subway tunnel, Rook finds the remains of a dog. A small one, with a collar like the one she found in the wheat field. She buries it in the tunnel wall and doesn't talk for a long time.
In the subway tunnel, there are marks on the wall. Scratches, like someone was counting days. There are hundreds of them.
The dog in the subway. Rook thinks about it later and realizes the dog was waiting. It wasn't dead; it was waiting for someone to come.
The subway platform is dry. There's a bench, a timetable, a ticket machine. Everything is as it was, preserved in the dark and the cold. As if no time has passed.
The counting scratches on the wall. Rook counts them. There are three hundred and sixty-five. One per day.

recall.hint: someone was trapped for a year

notes.content: The subway platform clock is running. It's not stopped like the water tower clock. It shows the correct time.
The subway platform clock shows 3:15. The same time as the wind-up clock in Sal's shack.
The subway platform clock shows 3:15. The same time as the wind-up clock in Sal's shack.

Sal realizes he's been here before. Not since the rain — before. He was in this subway station the week before the gray rain started. Waiting for a train that never came. He doesn't remember why he was waiting.

recall.hint: why Sal was waiting in the subway

notes.content: Rook sees Sal's expression and reaches out to touch his arm. He flinches. They've been traveling together for weeks and he still flinches at touch.
The breathing in the dark. Rook is afraid. She doesn't tell Sal.
At the end of the subway platform, in the dark beyond the lights, something is breathing. Slowly. Rhythmically. Not a machine.
The breathing in the dark is coming from a side tunnel. Rook follows it and finds a room. The room is full of people. They're sitting. They're alive. They're gray.

recall.hint: the gray people are in the subway

notes.content: One of the gray people looks up at Rook and smiles. It's an old woman. She knows Rook.

recall.hint: the old woman is her grandmother

notes.content: The people in the side tunnel. They're sitting in a circle. They're not looking at Rook; they're looking at the wall. At the counting scratches.
The old woman who knows Rook. She doesn't say anything; she just smiles and keeps looking at the wall.

They emerge from the subway at the base of the geology building. It's not collapsed like everything else. It's sealed. The entrance is a heavy steel door with a cylinder lock — the same lock that makes the click Sal heard on the radio. The same lock his B-7 key fits.
Sal holds the B-7 key up to the lock and his hand is shaking. He doesn't want to use it. Something in him knows what's on the other side.
The geology building door is warm because the pumps are running. The building is hot from the inside out.
Sal's fear. He knows what's inside. His hands shake as he holds the key.

Sal turns the key. The door unlocks with the familiar click. Inside, the geology building is not ruined. It's running. Lights, humming equipment, a smell of ozone and hot metal. Someone — or something — has been keeping it alive all these years.
Inside the geology building, the air is warm and smells of ozone. The hum is in his bones. Sal feels it in his teeth.
The hum in Sal's teeth. It's a low frequency, almost below hearing. It vibrates his whole body.

The geology building is a pump station. The gray rain wasn't a natural event — it was pumped down from above, deliberately, through a network of pipes that feed into every street, every drain, every building in the city. The wheat field map showed the pump network, not the drainage.
The pump station. Rook understands immediately. She's seen the pipes under the city streets. She's walked over them for years without knowing.
Rook understands the pipes. She's seen them because she's scavenged in the basements of buildings for years.
In the control room, Rook finds a wall of screens. One screen shows a live feed of the gas station. Another shows the library. Another shows the wheat field. They've been watched the whole time.
The camera network is extensive. There are cameras on every rooftop, every bridge, every street corner.
One screen shows the hilltop shack. The camera is looking at the seed library. Someone is watching the jars.

recall.hint: the seeds are the real experiment

notes.content: On the last screen is the blue door house. The family in Rook's photograph is sitting at their kitchen table, exactly as in the photo. They're not dead. They never left. And they're looking at a screen of their own — a screen that's showing Rook and Sal in the control room.
The family on the screen. They're eating dinner. They're laughing. They're normal, except for the gray.
The family on the screen. They're not just eating; they're watching the screen too. They're watching Rook.

In the control room, seated at a console, is a man Rook recognizes from her father's delivery journal. The man in the red pen address. Dr. Ellery. He's old now, gray and thin, but he's alive. And he's watching them.
Dr. Ellery is not surprised to see them. He says he's been waiting. He addresses Sal by name.
Dr. Ellery's hands are gray. All the way to the wrist. He's been experimenting on himself.

Dr. Ellery explains: the gray rain was an experiment. A soil treatment. The university was testing a new fertilizer compound that would grow crops faster in poor soil. It worked too well. It grew the wheat gray and then it killed everything else. They shut it down, but the pumps kept running on autopilot for three days after. Three days of gray rain.
Dr. Ellery's office is cluttered with papers. Years of notes, calculations, observations.
The experiment explanation. Rook listens and doesn't believe it. It doesn't add up. The soil treatment was a cover story.
Rook doesn't believe the soil treatment story. The math doesn't work. It would have killed everything, not just changed it.

Dr. Ellery knows about the letter Sal has been carrying for years. He says Dr. Ellery wrote it. It's not unsent — Sal sent it, years ago. He just doesn't remember. The letter was a thank you, for a test that went wrong and killed a woman named Mara.

The family at the blue door house are the experiment's first test subjects. They were the first to get the gray rain. They didn't die — they changed. Dr. Ellery has been keeping them in the house, studying them, for eight years. They are the first successful gray humans. And they are healthy. And they are happy. And they are growing.
The gray people in the house are growing plants in every room. The house is a garden now.

Dr. Ellery isn't the enemy. He's trying to fix it. The gray rain was an accident, but the gray people — he believes they're the future. They can survive in the poisoned soil. They can grow food. He's been trying to save everyone, the only way he knew how.
Sal burns another match. Five left. He counts them, and then he realizes something: he's burning them in sequence, and when the last one is gone, something ends. He's been counting down.
Sal burns a match. Four left. His hand is steady now. He knows what the matches mean.

recall.hint: the matches mark time or life

notes.content: Sal knows the matches count something important. He just doesn't know what.

Rook asks to see the gray people up close. Through the screen they look like everyone else. She's seen gray humans on the streets of the city — she thought they were feral. They weren't. They were hiding.
Rook asks to see a gray person up close. Through the screen they look like everyone else, but up close the gray is different. It's not color — it's texture. Their skin has the texture of bark.
The gray skin texture. Rook touches it and it feels like old paper. Dry and strong.
The photograph in Rook's jacket. She takes it out and studies it. The family's faces are slightly gray. She missed it before. They've been changing all along, in the photo, in her pocket.
Rook touches her own forearm, where the gravity scar is. The scar is slightly gray. She's been changing too. She doesn't remember when it started. She doesn't know how far it's gone.
The gray spreading from Rook's scar. She can see it move, very slowly, like a tide.

Dr. Ellery shows them the experiment's original proposal. The soil treatment wasn't designed to make plants grow faster. It was designed to make humans adapt to a poisoned environment. The wheat was just the test subject. The real experiment is everyone in the city.
The wall of photographs. The earliest ones show the family before the rain, looking normal. The later ones show the gray appearing.

Sal's half-finished letter. Dr. Ellery reads it aloud. It's not a thank-you letter. It's a confession. Sal was at the university because he was one of the engineers. He helped design the soil treatment. He doesn't remember because the gray rain affects memory first.
The family has always been gray. Rook remembers now. She forgot, but she remembers.

The gray rain doesn't just poison. It changes. And it changes first what you remember, then what you are. Sal forgot because he's already partially gray. He's been partially gray for eight years, walking the hills, tending his seeds, not knowing.
Sal's understanding. He helped build this machine that's changing the world, and he doesn't feel guilty. He feels like a scientist watching an experiment succeed.
The gray rain affects memory first. Sal realizes why he's been talking to his empty milk bowl and rolling empty cigarettes. The gray is in him, changing him from the inside.
The gray is in Sal too. He's been gray for eight years and he just found out.

Dr. Ellery offers them a choice. The pump station can be shut down. The gray rain will stop. But the gray people — the family, the ones on the streets — will sicken and die. The gray is in them now; it's not a poison to them anymore, it's them. Shut the pumps and you save the uninfected but you kill the changed.
The choice is simple but impossible. Save the old world or save the new people.
Sal holds the tin of matches. He has one more match left. He burns it. Four left. He doesn't know what it means yet, but his body knows. His hands are shaking.

recall.hint: what happens when the last match burns

notes.content: Sal thinks about the cat and the empty bowl. He's been keeping something alive for eight years that isn't there.

Rook doesn't speak. She opens her jacket, takes out the photograph of the family, and for the first time in eight years she recognizes them. Her father. Her mother. Her sister June. They're alive, gray, in the house at 14 Maple. June is there. She's alive and gray and waiting.
June's words: 'We've been waiting.' Rook understands now. Her sister has been waiting for her to find her, to come home. The gray didn't kill her; it kept her alive, waiting.
June's words echo in Rook's mind. 'We've been waiting.' Waiting for what? For Rook to find her. For Rook to come home.

They leave the geology building. They walk back up through the city, through the library, across the dead wheat field. But now the field is different. It's not gray anymore. New growth is pushing through. Green shoots, everywhere. The wheat is growing back green, because the pumps are still running, and the soil is being treated, and something is growing.
The green shoots in the wheat field. They're not just growing — they're growing fast, visibly fast. Rook watches and the green spreads across the field like a wave.
The green wave spreading across the wheat field. It's beautiful and terrifying. It's the future.
Sal's tin of matches. He opens it. It's empty. All the matches are burned. He looks at his hands and they are steady now. He is not afraid.
The empty match tin. Sal puts it in his pocket. He doesn't need it anymore.
The empty match tin. Sal puts it in his pocket. He doesn't need it anymore.

The brass compass. It works again. It points to the blue door house. Sal has never been to the blue door house, but the compass knows. It's been waiting for this moment, waiting for the gray to clear enough for it to work again.
needle_syns: points to the blue door house

notes.content: The compass leads them through the green field. The stalks brush past them, not like fingers now but like a blessing.

They arrive at the blue door house. It's the same as in the photograph. The door is blue. The door is open. Inside, at the kitchen table, the family is waiting. They are gray. They are smiling. June stands up and walks toward Rook, and she says, 'We've been waiting. We knew you'd come.'
The blue door is open. They're expected.
Rook reaches out and touches June's arm. The gray skin is warm. It's alive. It's her sister. She has her sister back.
The kitchen table. The same table as in the photograph. But now it's set for four, not three.
Rook touches June and the warmth is real. Her sister is real. All of them are real.

Sal stands at the door, not going in. He looks at Rook and then at the family. He says, 'I'll wait outside.' He walks out into the garden and sits on a bench. The wind-up clock on the wall of the house is running again. It's not 3:15 anymore. It's the right time.
Sal on the garden bench. He's not sad. He's not happy. He's watching the green wheat field and he feels something he hasn't felt in eight years. He feels present.
Sal on the bench. He's watching the green field and he feels at peace. For the first time in eight years.

On the garden bench, Sal opens his field book. On the last page, in his own handwriting, there's an entry he doesn't remember writing. It's dated today. It says: 'The experiment is complete. The subjects have adapted. Begin phase two.'
The phase two entry. His hand wrote it because his hand knows the truth. He helped build this and he'll help build what comes next.

The hand-crank radio, sitting on the kitchen table, crackles. The clear band is open. Something is saying, in a voice that is not Sal's and not Rook's: 'Phase one complete. Phase two beginning. Stand by.'
The ending should be quiet. No triumph. Just the radio, and the voice, and Rook looking at her gray hands, and Sal sitting on the bench, and the wheat field green in the distance.
The radio crackles. The voice is calm and patient. It has been waiting a long time to say this.
